section: Conflict and harmony between Fundamental Rights and DPSP - Champakam, Golaknath, Kesavananda, Minerva Mills
subsections: Article 39(b) and (c) laws - protection from Articles 14 and 19
Harmonious construction; Part III-Part IV balance as basic structure
Material resources of the community - latest SC view

accepted.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the justiciability of Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles of State Policy?
o: Fundamental Rights are non-enforceable, whereas Directive Principles are enforceable
Fundamental Rights are enforceable, whereas Directive Principles are non-enforceable
Both are enforceable by courts in the same manner
Neither Fundamental Rights nor Directive Principles is recognised by courts
accepted.x: Fundamental Rights are justiciable and can be enforced through courts. Directive Principles are non-justiciable under Article 37, though they are fundamental in the governance of the country.
accepted.tq: Test the central FR–DPSP distinction by separating enforceability from constitutional importance.
accepted.sec: FR vs DPSP - differences

accepted.s: The Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles respectively derive their conceptual sources from which of the following countries?
o: United Kingdom and Canada
United States of America and Ireland
Canada and Australia
Ireland and United States of America
accepted.x: The source of Fundamental Rights is the Constitution of the United States of America, whereas the Directive Principles were inspired by the Constitution of Ireland.
accepted.tq: Use the source-country pair as a direct constitutional comparison.
accepted.sec: FR vs DPSP - differences

accepted.s: Which of the following best expresses the difference in the general nature of Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles?
o: Fundamental Rights are mainly positive commands, while Directive Principles mainly restrain the State
Directive Principles impose criminal liability, while Fundamental Rights impose civil liability
Fundamental Rights mainly restrain the State, while Directive Principles direct the State towards positive action
Both Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles are mainly negative restrictions on the State
accepted.x: Fundamental Rights are mostly negative in character because they restrain State action. Directive Principles are positive directions intended to guide the State in promoting welfare.
accepted.tq: Discriminate between negative restraints and positive directions rather than between enforceability alone.
accepted.sec: FR vs DPSP - differences

accepted.s: Fundamental Rights primarily aim at political democracy and individual welfare, whereas Directive Principles primarily aim at
o: administrative centralisation and official privilege
judicial supremacy and territorial expansion
electoral competition and political party regulation
social and economic democracy and community welfare
accepted.x: Fundamental Rights emphasise political democracy and individual welfare. Directive Principles seek social and economic democracy along with community welfare.
accepted.tq: Match each constitutional part with its stated democratic and welfare objective.
accepted.sec: FR vs DPSP - differences

accepted.s: A law violating a Fundamental Right and a law violating a Directive Principle have which respective legal consequences?
o: The former may be void under Article 13, while the latter cannot be struck down merely for violating a Directive Principle
The former cannot be examined by courts, while the latter is void under Article 37
Both laws are automatically void under Article 13
Both laws are immune from judicial review
accepted.x: Article 13 makes laws inconsistent with Fundamental Rights void to the extent of inconsistency. Courts cannot strike down a law solely because it violates a Directive Principle.
accepted.tq: Apply the constitutional consequence separately to an enforceable right and a non-justiciable directive.
accepted.sec: FR vs DPSP - differences

accepted.s: With reference to the constitutional status of Directive Principles, which one of the following statements is correct?
o: They are legally superior to all Fundamental Rights in every circumstance
They are enforceable only during a national emergency
They have no constitutional significance because Article 37 excludes them from governance
They are not enforceable in courts but are fundamental in the governance of the country
accepted.x: Directive Principles are non-justiciable, but Article 37 declares them fundamental in the governance of the country and makes it the duty of the State to apply them in making laws.
accepted.tq: Avoid the trap of equating non-enforceability with lack of constitutional importance.
accepted.sec: FR vs DPSP - differences

accepted.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. The Forty-Second Amendment attempted to extend Article 31C protection to laws implementing all Directive Principles.
2. The Forty-Fourth Amendment gave all Directive Principles precedence over Articles 14 and 19.
3. The attempt to give all Directive Principles such precedence was struck down by the Supreme Court.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
o: 1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3
accepted.x: Statements 1 and 3 are correct. The Forty-Second Amendment, not the Forty-Fourth, attempted to extend Article 31C to all Directive Principles, and that extension was struck down.
accepted.tq: Catch the amendment-year swap by identifying which amendment made the attempt and which did not.
accepted.sec: Article 39(b) and (c) laws - protection from Articles 14 and 19

accepted.s:
The Forty-Second Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976 was associated with which of the following measures?
1. Extending Article 31C protection to laws implementing all Directive Principles
2. Claiming unlimited amending power under Article 368
3. Giving precedence to all Directive Principles over Articles 14 and 19
Which of the above is/are correct?
o: 1 only
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3
accepted.x: The Forty-Second Amendment attempted all three measures. The extension of Article 31C and the claim of unlimited amending power were subsequently invalidated in the relevant constitutional litigation.
accepted.tq: Recognise a cluster of provisions associated with one amendment instead of isolating only its best-known feature.
accepted.sec: Article 39(b) and (c) laws - protection from Articles 14 and 19

accepted.s: Which of the following was held in Minerva Mills v. Union of India?
o: Parliament possesses unlimited power to amend the Constitution
All Directive Principles automatically override Articles 14, 19 and 21
The balance between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles is a basic feature, and Parliament's limited amending power is itself basic
Article 31C was completely removed from the Constitution
accepted.x: Minerva Mills held that limited amending power is a basic feature and that harmony between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles is essential. The expansion of Article 31C to all Directive Principles was struck down, while its application to Article 39(b) and (c) survived.
accepted.tq: Use the basic-structure trap: an amendment cannot destroy the Constitution's own limited amending power.
accepted.sec: Article 39(b) and (c) laws - protection from Articles 14 and 19

accepted.s: Which one of the following additional propositions was recognised in Minerva Mills in relation to an Emergency proclamation?
o: It is subject only to review by the Election Commission
It can be reviewed only by a joint sitting of Parliament
It is permanently beyond judicial review
It is subject to judicial review
accepted.x: Minerva Mills recognised that an Emergency proclamation is not wholly immune from judicial review.
accepted.tq: Identify the constitutional authority involved in reviewing an executive emergency action.
accepted.sec: Article 39(b) and (c) laws - protection from Articles 14 and 19

accepted.s: After the decision in Minerva Mills, the relationship between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles is best described as one in which
o: Directive Principles permanently prevail over Fundamental Rights in every matter
Fundamental Rights permanently prevail over Directive Principles in every matter
both are complementary and form an integrated constitutional scheme
both are independent and cannot be read together
accepted.x: Minerva Mills rejected the idea of an absolute conflict and treated Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles as complementary components of an integrated constitutional scheme.
accepted.tq: Use the harmonious-construction approach instead of assuming an absolute hierarchy.
accepted.sec: Harmonious construction; Part III-Part IV balance as basic structure

accepted.s: The statement “Fundamental Rights are the means and Directive Principles are the ends” signifies that
o: Fundamental Rights provide the framework through which the social and economic objectives of Directive Principles may be pursued
Directive Principles have no relationship with Fundamental Rights
Fundamental Rights may be suspended whenever a Directive Principle is invoked
Directive Principles are enforceable through the same remedies as Fundamental Rights
accepted.x: Fundamental Rights provide rights-based means, while Directive Principles express broader social and economic goals. The two are therefore to be understood together, not as competing constitutional compartments.
accepted.tq: Translate a constitutional maxim into its practical relationship between rights and goals.
accepted.sec: Harmonious construction; Part III-Part IV balance as basic structure

accepted.s:
Which of the following illustrates the use of a Directive Principle as an interpretive aid to expand the content of a Fundamental Right?
1. Article 45 read with Article 21 contributed to the recognition of the Right to Education under Article 21A.
2. Article 48A read with Article 21 supports the right to a healthy environment.
3. Directive Principles are entirely excluded from constitutional interpretation because they are non-justiciable.
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
o: 1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3
accepted.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Courts have used Directive Principles to interpret and enrich Fundamental Rights; non-justiciability does not exclude them from constitutional interpretation.
accepted.tq: Distinguish non-enforceability from non-relevance in constitutional interpretation.
accepted.sec: Harmonious construction; Part III-Part IV balance as basic structure

accepted.s: In testing the validity of a law based on a Directive Principle but alleged to abridge Fundamental Rights, the relevant constitutional standard includes
o: the non-justiciability of Directive Principles alone
only Article 37, without reference to Fundamental Rights
only Article 32 and the Ninth Schedule
the basic structure doctrine and the golden triangle of Articles 14, 19 and 21
accepted.x: The validity of such a law is examined against the basic structure doctrine and, in particular, the constitutional guarantees represented by Articles 14, 19 and 21, known as the golden triangle.
accepted.tq: Apply the controlling constitutional test rather than treating a DPSP objective as conclusive.
accepted.sec: Harmonious construction; Part III-Part IV balance as basic structure

accepted.s:
Consider the following pairs:
1. Kesavananda Bharati — Amendments, including Ninth Schedule inclusions, cannot destroy the basic structure
2. Waman Rao — Post-24 April 1973 Ninth Schedule entries can be tested against the basic structure
3. I.R. Coelho — Every Ninth Schedule entry enjoys blanket immunity from judicial review
Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
o: 1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3
accepted.x: Pairs 1 and 2 are correctly matched. I.R. Coelho rejected blanket immunity and held that post-1973 entries may be invalid if they damage the basic structure or the essence of Articles 14, 19 and 21.
accepted.tq: Find the reversed proposition in a case-law match, especially where a judgment rejected an absolute rule.
accepted.sec: Harmonious construction; Part III-Part IV balance as basic structure

accepted.s:
Arrange the following decisions in chronological order:
A. I.R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu
B. Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala
C. Waman Rao v. Union of India
D. Minerva Mills v. Union of India
o: B, D, C, A
B, C, D, A
C, B, D, A
D, B, C, A
accepted.x: The correct sequence is Kesavananda Bharati (1973), Waman Rao (1981), Minerva Mills (1980), I.R. Coelho (2007) only if arranged by the dates stated? Actually Minerva Mills was decided in 1980 and therefore precedes Waman Rao. The correct chronological order is Kesavananda Bharati (1973), Minerva Mills (1980), Waman Rao (1981), I.R. Coelho (2007).
accepted.tq: Fix the dates first and then order the cases, paying particular attention to the close 1980–1981 sequence.
accepted.sec: Harmonious construction; Part III-Part IV balance as basic structure

accepted.s: Which one of the following statements regarding the Ninth Schedule is NOT correct?
o: Article 31B was inserted by the First Constitutional Amendment Act, 1951
The Ninth Schedule has remained confined to land reform laws and never expanded beyond them
The number of entries in it grew to more than 280
The Ninth Schedule was initially associated with protection for land reform laws from Fundamental Rights challenges
accepted.x: Statement c is not correct. Although the Ninth Schedule was initially intended for land reforms, its entries later grew to more than 280 and were not confined to that subject.
accepted.tq: Reject the absolute claim that an initially limited constitutional device never expanded.
accepted.sec: Harmonious construction; Part III-Part IV balance as basic structure

accepted.s: What was the significance of the cut-off date of 24 April 1973 laid down in Waman Rao?
o: Only laws enacted after the Forty-Fourth Amendment could be reviewed
All laws included in the Ninth Schedule before that date were automatically void
The date marked the commencement of Article 31C
Ninth Schedule entries made after that date could be tested against the basic structure
accepted.x: Waman Rao treated 24 April 1973 as the cut-off date and held that Ninth Schedule laws or entries added after it could be examined against the basic structure.
accepted.tq: Use the date as a legal cut-off rather than confusing it with the date of an amendment or provision.
accepted.sec: Harmonious construction; Part III-Part IV balance as basic structure

accepted.s: The decision in I.R. Coelho is significant because it held that
o: Ninth Schedule laws are completely beyond judicial review
only laws relating to land reforms can be placed in the Ninth Schedule
post-1973 Ninth Schedule entries may be invalid if they damage the basic structure or the essence of Articles 14, 19 and 21
Article 31B was repealed in its entirety
accepted.x: I.R. Coelho rejected blanket immunity. Post-1973 Ninth Schedule entries remain open to review if they damage the basic structure or the essential guarantees of Articles 14, 19 and 21.
accepted.tq: Identify the exception to immunity by connecting Ninth Schedule review with the golden triangle.
accepted.sec: Harmonious construction; Part III-Part IV balance as basic structure

accepted.s: Justice Chandrachud described Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles together as constituting the
o: code of administrative procedure
exclusive domain of the executive
conscience of the Constitution
framework of parliamentary privilege
accepted.x: Justice Chandrachud described Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles together as making up the conscience of the Constitution.
accepted.tq: Recall the distinctive judicial phrase attached to the combined constitutional role of Parts III and IV.
accepted.sec: Harmonious construction; Part III-Part IV balance as basic structure

accepted.s: Which of the following correctly states the latest Supreme Court position on the expression “material resources of the community” in Article 39(b)?
o: No privately owned resource can ever be a material resource of the community
Only resources owned by the Union Government can be covered
Whether a privately owned resource is covered depends on factors such as its nature, scarcity, effect on community well-being and the consequences of concentration in private hands
Every privately owned resource is automatically a material resource of the community
accepted.x: In Property Owners Association v. State of Maharashtra, the Supreme Court held that private ownership alone does not automatically bring a resource within Article 39(b). The determination depends on the resource and its effects on the community and concentration of wealth.
accepted.tq: Apply the latest multi-factor judicial test instead of choosing an absolute public-versus-private rule.
accepted.sec: Material resources of the community - latest SC view

accepted.s: Property Owners Association v. State of Maharashtra, decided on 5 November 2024, was decided by
o: a nine-judge Bench unanimously
a seven-judge Bench unanimously
a five-judge Bench by a 3:2 majority
a nine-judge Bench by a 7:2 majority
accepted.x: The case was decided on 5 November 2024 by a nine-judge Bench, with the relevant conclusion being reached by a 7:2 majority.
accepted.tq: Separate Bench strength from the majority ratio when handling a recent constitutional judgment.
accepted.sec: Material resources of the community - latest SC view

accepted.s: In Property Owners Association v. State of Maharashtra, the majority view was delivered by
o: Justice Y.V. Chandrachud as a dissenting judge
Chief Justice P.N. Bhagwati
Justice Krishna Iyer
Chief Justice D.Y. Chandrachud
accepted.x: The majority opinion in the November 2024 nine-judge Bench decision was delivered by Chief Justice D.Y. Chandrachud.
accepted.tq: Avoid the judge-name trap by distinguishing the current majority opinion from the earlier Krishna Iyer view.
accepted.sec: Material resources of the community - latest SC view

accepted.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the judicial history of Article 39(b):
1. In State of Karnataka v. Ranganatha Reddy (1977), Justice Krishna Iyer's minority view included privately owned resources within “material resources of the community”.
2. The broad view was followed in Sanjeev Coke (1983).
3. Property Owners Association rejected the proposition that every privately owned resource automatically falls within Article 39(b).
Which of the statements given above are correct?
o: 1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3
accepted.x: All three statements are correct. The broad interpretation associated with Justice Krishna Iyer in Ranganatha Reddy was followed in Sanjeev Coke, while the 2024 Property Owners Association decision rejected its automatic application to every privately owned resource.
accepted.tq: Track the evolution of a legal proposition from an earlier minority view to its later qualification.
accepted.sec: Material resources of the community - latest SC view

accepted.s: Which one of the following is NOT correctly matched?
o: Sanjeev Coke — 1983
Property Owners Association — 2024
Waman Rao — 2007
Ranganatha Reddy — 1977
accepted.x: Waman Rao was decided in 1981, not 2007. I.R. Coelho was the 2007 decision concerning the absence of blanket immunity for Ninth Schedule entries.
accepted.tq: Use the year mismatch to distinguish closely related constitutional cases.
accepted.sec: Material resources of the community - latest SC view
